title: Endoscopic Management of Pancreaticojejunostomy Leak and Dehiscence After Pancreatoduodenectomy: An Anatomy-Driven Multidisciplinary Framework
content: Pancreaticojejunostomy (PJ) leak after pancreatoduodenectomy is graded by the International Study Group of Pancreatic Surgery (ISGPS) postoperative pancreatic fistula (POPF) definition, which captures clinical relevance but not the anatomical target to be treated. This structured narrative review examines endoscopic management of PJ leak and dehiscence and proposes complementary, computed tomography (CT)-informed phenotypes: biochemical leak without an actionable target (Phenotype 1); persistent external fistula without a drainable collection (Phenotype 2); drainable collection with preserved apposition (Phenotype 3); and complete loss of PJ apposition (Phenotype 4), subdivided by remnant perfusion (4a/4b). These phenotypes are hypothesis-generating and unvalidated. The corresponding objectives are observation, fistula internalization, collection source control and pancreatic diversion. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided drainage, transanastomotic and pancreatic-duct interventions, lumen-apposing metal stents, rendezvous and vacuum-based techniques should be integrated with interventional radiology and surgery according to anatomy and physiological stability, after delayed haemorrhage has been excluded or controlled. Evidence on reconstruction technique, operative approach, stents, drains, risk scores, radiomics and artificial intelligence is also summarized: none removes the need for structured surveillance, and no prediction tool yet addresses structural dehiscence. Evidence is largely retrospective. Prospective studies should test whether combining ISGPS grade, CT-defined anatomy and microbiology improves selection for minimally invasive rescue.
